chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, he said:
I said to him: A man performs ghusl with rose-water and performs wudu (ablution) with it for salat (prayer)? He said: There is no harm in that.

So this is an anomalous report, extremely anomalous. Even if it is repeated in the books, its source is only Yūnus from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, and no one besides him narrated it. The group has agreed upon abandoning acting according to its apparent meaning, and whatever is of this status is not acted upon.

And even if it were established, it could be that what is meant by wudu (ablution) in the report is beautification. We have already explained in our book Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām the discussion concerning that, and that this is called wudu in the language.

And no one has the right to say that the report states that he asked him about rose-water with which he performs wudu (ablution) for salat (prayer) and performs ghusl with it, because that does not contradict what we have said. For it is permissible that it be used for beautification, while along with that entry into salat (prayer) is intended by it, inasmuch as whenever a pleasant fragrance is used for entering into salat (prayer), that is better than intending by it only perfuming oneself and enjoyment, apart from the sake of Allah, Exalted is He.

And his saying, 'he performs ghusl with it,' may mean the lifting of prohibition from using it in ghusl and the negation of extravagance concerning it, even though seeking permissibility for salat (prayer) by means of it is not valid.

And it is also possible that what is meant by his saying 'rose-water' is water into which roses had fallen, because that is called rose-water even if it was not pressed from them. For everything that is adjacent to something else acquires from it a relational name, if adjacency is what is intended by it, as they say: the water of the jar, the water of the well, the water of the reservoir, and the water of the waterskins. All of that is an attribution of adjacency, and in that is the invalidation of reliance upon the report.

key_terms.إِضَافَةُ مُجَاوَرَةٍ: a relational attribution based on adjacency or association
key_terms.اسْتِبَاحَةُ الصَّلَاةِ: the attainment of legal permissibility to enter salat (prayer)
key_terms.التَّحْسِينَ: beautification or adornment rather than ritual purification
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), here possibly interpreted in its linguistic sense of beautification
key_terms.خَبَرٌ شَاذٌّ: an anomalous hadith report not relied upon in its apparent sense

ai.seo_question: Can rose-water be used for wudu (ablution) and ghusl according to this hadith in al-Istibṣār?
ai.summary: This passage discusses a report about using rose-water for ghusl and wudu (ablution) for salat (prayer), then judges the report to be highly anomalous and not suitable for acting upon according to its apparent meaning. It further offers possible interpretations that preserve established legal principles, including understanding wudu here as beautification or understanding 'rose-water' as water merely associated with roses.
